Solution:
**Solution:**
We will prove that if S ⊆Rn is a polyhedron, then its polar set S◦is also a polyhedron.
**Definitions and Preliminaries:** 1. A **polyhedron** is the intersection of finitely
many half-spaces, i.e., it can be written as S = {x ∈Rn | Ax ≤b} for some matrix
A ∈Rm×n and vector b ∈Rm. 2. The **polar set** of S is defined as S◦= {y ∈Rn | yTx ≤
1 for all x ∈S}.
**Proof:**
Assume S is a polyhedron given by:
S = {x ∈Rn | Ax ≤b},
where A ∈Rm×n and b ∈Rm.
We want to show that S◦is also a polyhedron. By definition:
S◦= {y ∈Rn | yTx ≤1 for all x such that Ax ≤b}.
Using duality, the condition yTx ≤1 for all x satisfying Ax ≤b can be rephrased using
Farkas’ Lemma or linear programming duality. Specifically, yTx ≤1 for all x with Ax ≤b
holds if and only if there exists a non-negative vector λ ∈Rm
+ such that:
ATλ = y
and
bTλ ≤1.
Thus, we can express S◦as:
S◦= {y ∈Rn | ∃λ ≥0 such that ATλ = y, bTλ ≤1}.
This is the projection onto the y-variables of the polyhedron defined by:
{(y, λ) ∈Rn × Rm | ATλ = y, bTλ ≤1, λ ≥0}.
Since projections of polyhedra are polyhedra (by the Fourier-Motzkin elimination process
or the Minkowski-Weyl theorem), it follows that S◦is a polyhedron.
Alternatively, we can write S◦explicitly as the intersection of half-spaces derived from
the inequalities defining S. For each row aT
i of A, the condition aT
i x ≤bi implies that for
y ∈S◦, we must have yTx ≤1 for all x satisfying aT
i x ≤bi.
If bi > 0, the maximum of yTx subject to aT
i x ≤bi is yT ai
bi
(achieved at x = ai
bi ), so we
must have yT ai
bi
≤1, i.e., yTai ≤bi.
If bi = 0, the condition aT
i x ≤0 must hold for all x ∈S, and yTx ≤1 for all such x
implies y must be in the recession cone of S, i.e., yTx ≤0 for all x with aT
i x ≤0. This is
equivalent to y being a non-negative multiple of ai, i.e., y = λai for some λ ≥0.
Combining these observations, S◦can be written as:
S◦= {y ∈Rn | yTai ≤bi for all i with bi > 0}∩{y ∈Rn | y = λai, λ ≥0 for all i with bi = 0}.
This is a finite intersection of half-spaces and lines (which can also be expressed as half-
spaces), hence S◦is a polyhedron.
**Conclusion:**
We have shown that the polar set S◦of a polyhedron S is itself a polyhedron, either by
duality arguments or by explicitly constructing its half-space representation.
S◦is a polyhedron

fields.explanation: Original vectors(1,0),(0,1),(0,3),(1,1),(2,0) and original setsSbox={x1≤1,x2≤1},Sprime={2x1≤1} are retained. Mathlib dotProduct evaluates the same inner products. Universal real one-sided polar membership is proved directly; the absolute polar library definition is intentionally not substituted because it changes the source notion. The selected theorem certifies the source-qualified primary counterexample. Historical auxiliary sweeps are not silently promoted to universal statements. The scaled-row convex-hull formula additionally requires every b_i>0; merely0∈S does not make division by b_i legitimate. The original per-row argument also permits x=(0,N) for every real N>0: a1·x=0≤1 and y·x=N>0, contradicting the asserted value zero. Taking arbitrarily large N proves that this row objective is unbounded above; the same a1, b1 and y are retained.
fields.flaw: Keep all three original real-plane constructions. (A) For a1=(1,0), b1=1 and y=(0,1), the point x=(0,3) satisfies a1·x≤1 but y·x=3>0=y·a1/b1, refuting the claimed row maximum. Also y belongs to the polar of S={x1≤1,x2≤1}. (B) For this S, y=(1,1) satisfies both proposed row inequalities, but x=(1,1) belongs to S and y·x=2>1, so y is not in the true polar. (C) For S′={2x1≤1}, y=(1,0) belongs to the true polar because x1≤1/2≤1 for every x in S′, yet y·(2,0)=2>1. The selected Lean theorem uses universal real one-sided polar membership and Mathlib dotProduct. The original per-row argument also permits x=(0,N) for every real N>0: a1·x=0≤1 and y·x=N>0, contradicting the asserted value zero. Taking arbitrarily large N proves that this row objective is unbounded above; the same a1, b1 and y are retained.

Problem Statement
Problem: Algorithms - 43
Let S ⊆Rn. Define the polar set S◦by S◦:= {y ∈Rn | yTx ≤1 for every x ∈S}. Prove
that if S is a polyhedron, then S◦is necessarily a polyhedron as well.
1
